analysis.one_liner: Sends working families a monthly tax credit and closes tax loopholes used by billionaires.
analysis.headline: A freshman Democrat's bill to pay working families a monthly tax credit and tax billionaires' loopholes has no cosponsors and sits untouched in the tax-writing committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code to send a credit to working Americans every month instead of once a year at tax time, and would close loopholes that let billionaires avoid tax on their wealth. That money would come from the very top of the wealth scale. It was introduced in mid-September 2026 by one House Democrat, referred to the tax-writing committee, and has attracted no cosponsors from either party since [S1][S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Working Americans who would receive a tax credit paid out monthly rather than once a year, making it usable for rent, groceries, and childcare as bills arrive rather than as a lump sum in the spring.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working Americans receiving monthly tax credits

how_it_helps.text: The bill would provide a refundable tax credit paid to working Americans every month, so the money arrives when household bills do, not once a year at tax filing [S1].
It would close tax loopholes available to billionaires, requiring the wealthiest households to pay tax on wealth they currently shelter from the income tax, which taxes mainly wages [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Billionaires and the wealthiest households, whose untaxed wealth would face new taxation; the revenue would fund the monthly credit.

drawbacks.text: Closing loopholes on billionaire wealth generally means taxing gains on assets that have not been sold, which requires valuing private companies, art, and land that have no market price, and can force asset sales to pay the tax — a real administrative objection even supporters must answer [S1].

A monthly credit paid during the year must later be reconciled against actual income at tax time; if a household's income rises during the year, some of the credit can come back owed, a problem the bill's text would need to address [S1].

The title ends with "and for other purposes," and the full scope of the bill's provisions is not evident from its title, so the complete cost and effect cannot be assessed from the public record alone [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and easy to see: working families get usable money monthly, funded by closing shelters available only at the very top of the wealth scale. The honest objections are practical — valuing unsold billionaire assets is hard, and monthly advance payments require careful reconciliation so families do not face surprise tax bills. The concept has been debated for years in other forms without becoming law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which decides whether tax bills get a hearing or a vote, and it has not moved since [S3].

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the bill on September 14, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S3].
No other member of the House — Democrat or Republican — has signed on as a cosponsor [S2].
The committee has taken no further action on the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet: the bill sits in committee, and the tax status quo — including the billionaire loopholes it targets — remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one — the bill sits untouched

for.name: Rep. Greg Landsman
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, on which he sits.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls have occurred and no member of either party has cosponsored, so the partisan shape is unknown; the only name on the bill is its Democratic sponsor [S2].

industries.note: The bill would close loopholes these households use to keep unrealized wealth out of the tax code; their gain under current law is revenue ordinary taxpayers otherwise shoulder [S1].

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since introduction late in the session, the bill is on the standard path of most one-sponsor tax bills: it will almost certainly die in committee without a hearing or a vote when the Congress ends in early January.
